title: You Don’t Own the Off Switch
body_text: Introduction At the risk of being too on the nose here: the real risk with frontier AI models is not always model quality, latency, or price. Sometimes the biggest risk is much simpler than that. Access can disappear. When a government can order access cut to a newly released, industry-leading model, it exposes a truth that many teams still treat as an implementation detail instead of a strategic risk. If your product, workflow, or customer delivery depends on a model served through a third-party API, then the infrastructure you are relying on is not actually yours. It belongs to someone else. You are renting access by the token, under terms and conditions you do not control. That distinction matters more than most teams want to admit. A model that powers critical workflows can be deprecated, rate-limited, restricted by geography, or shut off altogether. And when that happens, the impact is not theoretical. It hits operations, delivery timelines, customer commitments, and product reliability all at once. The lesson is not that frontier models are bad. The lesson is that depending on access you do not control is a fragile foundation for anything mission-critical. The Vendor API Was Never Your Infrastructure There is a common habit in AI product planning: treating a vendor API as though it were a stable infrastructure layer. If it works well today, teams start designing around the assumption that it will still be there tomorrow, under roughly the same rules, with roughly the same performance. But that assumption is doing far too much work. A vendor API is not the same as infrastructure you own or govern. It is a service relationship. The model may be world-class. The API may be robust. The documentation may be excellent. None of that changes the fact that the underlying access is conditional. That conditionality becomes easy to ignore when everything is working. Teams move fast. Features ship. Dependencies settle into the background. The model becomes embedded in internal processes and customer-facing experiences. Over time, what began as convenient external tooling turns into a critical operational dependency. The problem is that the control never moved with it. If the vendor changes terms, your roadmap changes. If the vendor changes limits, your throughput changes. If the vendor loses permission to serve a model, your product changes. In every case, the dependency remains yours to absorb, but not yours to govern. That is the heart of the issue. You may have built the workflow. You may have integrated the model deeply. You may be paying real money at meaningful scale. But if someone else controls whether access exists tomorrow, then you do not control the system as much as you think you do. Business Continuity Is Being Set Somewhere Else Most companies take business continuity seriously when it comes to databases, cloud regions, backups, or authentication. They understand the need for failover, redundancy, and control over critical systems. Yet many of those same companies treat model access as if it sits outside that discipline. It does not. If a model is central to decision-making, automation, labeling, summarization, generation, or any other business-critical workflow, then access to that model is part of your operational continuity. And if that continuity depends on external policy decisions made by institutions you do not answer to, through vendors you do not control, then your risk posture is weaker than it appears. This is what makes model access different from a normal feature dependency. The failure mode is not just technical. It is also regulatory, contractual, geopolitical, and organizational. A change can happen far upstream from your team, with no meaningful seat for you in the decision. That means your continuity planning cannot stop at “the API is up.” It has to extend to “what happens if access is revoked, constrained, or reprioritized?” If there is no strong answer to that question, then the business is operating on borrowed confidence. The risk is not hypothetical paranoia. It is structural exposure. “We’ll Just Swap Models” Is Often a Fantasy A common response to this concern is: fine, if one model becomes unavailable, we will just switch to another one. That sounds practical. In reality, it is often much less simple. Model swaps are rarely frictionless. Different models behave differently under the same prompts. They vary in reasoning patterns, output formats, latency, tool use, reliability, safety behavior, and domain performance. Teams that say they can “just swap” are often assuming a level of portability that has not actually been tested under production conditions. And even if the technical swap is possible, the timing may not be. Critical workflows are rarely interrupted at convenient moments. If access changes overnight, the organization may be forced into a rushed transition rather than a controlled one. That means engineering time gets redirected, QA gets compressed, stakeholders get nervous, and customers may feel the instability before the internal team has even finished adapting. More importantly, “we’ll just swap” still assumes the swap is yours to make. But if your operating model depends entirely on external access to whichever vendor is currently available, then you are not solving the control problem. You are only moving it around. The issue is not whether alternatives exist. The issue is whether your organization can move between them on its own terms, at its own pace, with its own safeguards. If not, then you are still exposed. Private Deployment Is No Longer a Nice-to-Have This is why private deployment matters so much now. Private deployment changes the control surface. It does not eliminate all risk, and it does not make every model decision easy. But it does shift the core question from “are we still allowed to use this?” to “how do we want to operate this?” That is a fundamentally stronger position. When deployment is private, the organization has more control over continuity, governance, access, and change management. It can plan upgrades deliberately. It can define operating constraints based on its own needs. It can reduce exposure to sudden shifts in external availability. Most importantly, it can keep critical workflows tied to infrastructure decisions it actually has authority over. This is not an argument against frontier models. Frontier models can be extraordinarily valuable. They can unlock real performance gains and meaningful product improvements. The problem is not capability. The problem is dependency without control. That is why private deployment is no longer just a preference for security-conscious teams or highly regulated environments. It is increasingly the only serious option for organizations that want durable control over core AI workflows. Conclusion Frontier models are not the problem. Fragile access is. If your most important workflows depend on a model that can be deprecated, rate-limited, restricted, or shut off without your participation in the decision, then your system is more temporary than it looks. You may be building something powerful, but you are building it on top of an off switch you do not own. That is the real lesson here. The future of enterprise AI will not be defined only by which models are strongest. It will also be defined by who controls the conditions under which those models can continue to operate. For teams building serious products and serious workflows, that control is no longer optional. If you want reliability, continuity, and strategic freedom, private deployment is not just a nice-to-have. It is the version where you hold the reins.

title: How to Train Employees to Encourage Great Reviews | Superorder
summary: Elevate your restaurant's reputation by training employees to ensure guest satisfaction. Discover how this can lead to positive reviews and business success.
body_text: Cultivating a Culture of Guest Satisfaction: Employee Training for Review Success In the hospitality industry, success hinges on a great customer experience. There's no better example of that than restaurants. Restaurants require a constant stream of happy customers and positive reviews to succeed. Failing to meet the mark can ruin your business, especially when customers turn to the many online review sites to share their experiences with others. Countless touchpoints could negatively impact a customer's experience. For example, lackluster food or slow delivery service could sour the journey they have with your restaurant. While you can resolve those challenges to create more positive customer experiences, one approach that's making a huge difference in the hospitality industry is transforming the work culture. A customer-centric culture puts guests at the top of the priority totem pole. Instead of having a corporate culture that puts products above customers, all decisions and strategies revolve around customer service and satisfaction. In this blog, we'll discuss the importance of shifting your business toward a customer-centric culture and how you can make positive improvements that lead to long-term success. Why is it Important? Guest satisfaction is crucial to your success as a player in the hospitality industry. Restaurants do more than just serve food. They provide a full experience, and every facet of that experience can impact a guest's ultimate satisfaction. Your goal is to make customers feel that you provided great value. Otherwise, unhappy customers may spread their experience through reviews and word-of-mouth, harming your reputation and making it more difficult to attract new customers. Customer satisfaction should be at the heart of everything you do as a restaurant owner. Products and profits matter, but they won't mean much if you don't have customers to serve! A customer service culture puts the needs and expectations of your guests at the forefront. The approach can guide your decision-making, highlight metrics you need to improve and help you develop brand-new strategies for business success and a sky-high Net Promoter Score (NPS). Putting customers first can lead to great success for any business, but it makes a substantial difference for restaurants trying to sell an entire package. Not only will a customer service culture help your team deliver a great experience through impeccable customer interactions, but it can also reframe what's important for every other operation. That customer-centric approach can make it easier to avoid errors when preparing orders, delays when offering delivery service, dispute resolution when things don't go right and more. Understanding Common Guest Expectations The first step in adopting a customer-focused, high-performance company culture is to understand what your guests expect. Knowing what people expect from your restaurant allows you to develop strategies and model the customer journey to maximize satisfaction. Guests expect a few core things from a restaurant: great food, exceptional customer service and relatively quick service. However, these are just the basic expectations. The real challenge lies in understanding the nuances and complexities of expectations that can vary based on the type of restaurant you run. For example, some guests expect impeccable customer service and an impressive ambiance. They may also want a smooth online ordering process and fast delivery service. It's important to remember that expectations vary from one restaurant to another. Guests visiting a fast-food joint expect much less from employees than in a fine-dining establishment, and people will let much more slide in a low-cost casual dining environment. Consider your restaurant and the customer experience you're trying to sell. Put yourself in your guests' shoes to understand their expectations. But don't stop there. Shifting your company's core values to focus on guest satisfaction means not just meeting those expectations but exceeding them. This commitment to excellence is what sets high-performing restaurants apart. Importance of Imparting Excellent Customer Service Skills Good customer service is what matters most in the hospitality industry. The entire hospitality industry is customer-centric. You're providing a service and an experience that many other businesses offer. If you want your restaurant to rise to the top, you must give guests the best customer experience possible. Impressive customer service can impact the overall success of the company, so you must ingrain that into your staff. Putting the customer first should be one of your restaurant's core values, and all team members must contribute to the common goal of providing exceptional customer service. Customer service goes beyond putting on a smile, taking orders and waiting tables. It encompasses all customer interactions and impacts the larger experience for your guests. Good customer service means catering to your patrons' every need, working hard to ensure that dishes are prepared to perfection and that the overall experience is as perfect as you can make it. Adopting a customer-centric culture in your restaurant is the ticket to guest satisfaction. When you prioritize your customers' needs, that focus ripples across every part of your operation. It translates to more accurate food prep, faster order processing and more. The result is fewer mishaps that could sour the customer experience. Enhancing Employee Communication With Customers One of the key elements to cultivating a customer-centric culture is improving how your employees interact with customers. Invest in training and development programs. Development programs should lean into customer service skills, focusing on how your teams engage with customers. It should go beyond the ABCs of taking orders. A great customer service training program will teach employees how to make guests feel great while handling their needs to a tee! Development opportunities can make a huge difference for your team. In addition to teaching valuable and necessary skills, a great training program can change how servers, hosts and other customer-facing positions approach their jobs. Your frontline employees are the face of your business. Your job as a restaurant owner is to do more than put the right people in customer-facing positions. It's to train new hires and existing employees to develop exceptional customer service skills that elevate your business. Investing in development opportunities is investing in your team, and the payoff can lead to greater success, more revenue and lower employee turnover rates. Empathy and Problem Resolution Empathy plays a significant role in good customer service. When cultivating a customer service culture, you need people who empathize with others. Customer complaints happen. Mistakes will occur no matter how much you invest in training and how well-run your back-of-house operation is. It's the reality of the fast-paced restaurant and hospitality industry. What matters most is how your team members respond to incidents. With a customer-centric culture, your restaurant should go above and beyond to make things right. That means having empathy for the customer experience. Every team member, from a CEO to a server, should empathize with customers' issues. Empathy allows you to put yourself in your guests' shoes and develop meaningful resolutions. Sometimes, a simple apology isn't enough to correct the situation. When those situations occur, your team should have the skills, know-how and empathy to find a resolution that does make a difference. When developing a customer service culture, your goal is to make effective problem resolution second nature, ensuring that your team goes that extra mile to turn a negative experience into an outstanding one. Creating a Welcoming Atmosphere Of course, outstanding service doesn't stop with great interactions from your staff. You must also prioritize creating a welcoming environment. Customer loyalty hinges on whether or not guests feel valued and welcome at your establishment. Nothing will drive people away more than rushed or borderline rude interactions! A customer service culture means making people feel welcome before they ever set foot into your restaurant. Ambiance, great decor and chill music make a difference. But your efforts should go beyond all that. Greet customers with a smile. Guests should hear kind voices and an exciting tone when calling your restaurant to place an order or make reservations. The onboarding experience should be friction-free and welcoming when ordering on your app. Many factors can forge a positive experience. Consider all touchpoints and embrace kindness, empathy and hospitality throughout the organization. Providing Tools and Techniques for Managing Difficult Guest Interactions Disputes, mistakes and substandard service are bound to happen at some point. As mentioned earlier, what's important is how you respond to those situations. Your team members should know how to respond when difficult customer interactions occur. Train your staff on de-escalation techniques and problem resolution. You can also have protocols in place to resolve issues as soon as possible. That includes having techniques for frontline employees and going up the chain of command. You can also implement technology to help with dispute management. Technology can make a big difference when cultivating a customer service culture. Advanced software can help you navigate both in-person and digital interactions to mitigate issues and avoid complaints. Some platforms can also enhance productivity by providing real-time alerts to order errors, allowing your team to address the problems before they affect the customer experience. Problem resolution should be a top priority in a customer-centric culture. Train your team, develop strategies and techniques to address every worst-case scenario and do what you can to make things right for unhappy customers. Implementing Feedback Loops Leaning into a customer service culture shouldn't be a one-time thing. It needs to be continuous and ever-evolving. The restaurant industry continues to change, and patrons' needs and expectations will evolve over time. What works now might not work a year from now. So, how do you maintain a customer-centric culture? The best approach is to create and implement feedback loops. With a feedback loop, you gather customer insight to learn about what your restaurant does right and what needs improvement. It's a way to get honest feedback from your patrons while identifying areas of your operation that need improvement. Focus on the customer experience and gather opinions with customer surveys. Use what you learn from surveys to train customer service teams, adjust protocols and more. Then, continue to gather feedback to see what customers think of the changes. That continuous feedback loop can benefit customer service teams over the long haul. It helps your restaurant perfect the customer experience in every way while allowing you to stay ahead of the curve. Employee Recognition and Motivation Don't forget to recognize the hard work of your customer service teams and employees. A big part of having a customer service culture is acknowledging that your employees are integral to the overall success of your business. Frontline employees are the face of your restaurant, and their performance will impact guest satisfaction more than anything else. Strive to foster growth and empowerment in your team. A team that feels valued and motivated will go the extra mile to maintain your customer-centric culture and drive your business forward. Consider the importance of performance reviews, a tool that not only recognizes strengths but also identifies areas for improvement, leading to personal and professional growth. Acknowledge the good they do and offer professional development opportunities to address skill gaps or areas that need improvement. You can offer bonuses, foster teamwork for improvement, award dedication and more. Another thing you can do is accept employee feedback. Your frontline employees know your customers better than anyone; their input can make a huge difference. Not only can their input improve your customer-centric culture, but employee feedback also makes your team feel valued. Make your culture shift a collaborative effort! Recognize your team's contributions and allow everyone to shape your restaurant's guiding principles. Set clear goals, award hard work and create positive employee experiences. Before you know it, you'll notice increased productivity and much higher customer satisfaction scores. Continuous Training and Adaptation Feedback loops can help you find new opportunities to improve and evolve. Don't stop at collecting customer opinions. Many restaurants will invest time and resources into engaging customers and gathering feedback. However, many will hesitate to address concerns and implement changes. Cultivating a new workplace culture with customer-centricity isn't easy, so it's not hard to see why some restaurateurs are hesitant to push things further. But resting on your laurels in the hospitality industry can quickly leave you in the dust! Your rivals are always on your heels, so you should always strive for continuous improvement. This business constantly evolves. Continue to learn and grow. Gather customer feedback and use it to your advantage. Evolve your practices, cater to your changing customer base and always reach for the stars with customer service. The only way to grow in this industry is to push for excellence, and that push should be never-ending. Get Started With Superorder Today A customer service culture can make all the difference in your restaurant's long-term success. Guest satisfaction matters, so putting them first will improve every facet of your restaurant operation. Prioritizing positive customer experiences is key, and a customer-centric culture can make exceeding customer expectations second nature for every team member. Try our tips and see how much of a difference they can make. From shifting priorities to investing in employee training, small changes will accumulate to a brand-new work culture that will put you on the path to great success. It includes many game-changing features to help your business lean into customer-centricity. These include feedback management tools, real-time order monitoring, AI-powered review management and more. Check out Superorder today to learn more and discover a new way to manage your restaurant.

title: Elementary 2.0: Trusted Data for the AI Era
summary: Elementary 2.0 is the Enterprise Data & AI Control Plane that unifies observability, governance, and discovery, helping teams scale data and AI products with confidence.
body_text: Most data teams are feeling the same pressure right now: AI is advancing rapidly, expectations are rising even faster, and the foundations were not built for this level of scale. Elementary 2.0 is our response. It is a data and AI control plane that brings data engineering, data science, and analytics teams into one place so they can scale data and AI products with confidence. At the center is a shared context engine and a network of AI agents that handle observability, quality, governance, and discovery. Everything is designed so data reliability is something the system maintains, not something teams chase. We will be hosting a live session that walks through the new capabilities of Elementary 2.0, sign up for the webinar. Why we built the Enterprise Data & AI Control Plane Leveraging AI is no longer limited by the quality of models. Models are already strong and useful. The real blockers are upstream. AI demands solid foundations. If the inputs and definitions behind data and metrics are shaky, trust collapses and adoption stalls. AI demands more context. LLMs are only as good as the data and metadata you provide them. AI demands more data, faster. Pipelines, data products, and dependencies grow faster than any team can keep up with manually. Data teams are doing heroic work, but the workload scales faster than headcount. Data tests need maintenance. Data incidents need investigation. Pull requests need impact analysis. Documentation needs upkeep. Naming, tagging, lineage, performance tuning, cost reviews, it all compounds. The gap is structural. The control plane is meant to close that gap. It gives every part of the data team one shared understanding of lineage, tests, incidents, performance, definitions, and usage, and layers AI on top so reliability becomes proactive instead of reactive. What changes with Elementary 2.0 An end-to-end context engine at the core Everything starts with a unified layer of observability and metadata, built on our open core. It learns continuously from lineage, test results, incidents, performance signals, semantics, and usage patterns. That context powers AI agents and gives every team, and every workflow, the same understanding of what the data is, how it is built, and whether it is healthy. Because the engine is open core, all metadata stays in the customer’s environment, and data teams can customize it, extend it, and build their own dashboards or agents on top. We’re extending this engine in two major ways: 1. Monitoring Python pipelines and workloads Data teams can now capture context and metadata from any Python workload. That includes ingestion before data lands in a platform, Python jobs that consume data downstream, analytical and data science workloads, and AI pipelines written in Python. It can also capture results from existing test frameworks like Great Expectations and DQX. 2. Coverage across all major cloud data platforms and data lakes Elementary now monitors and captures metadata on any data asset in data warehouses and lakes like Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, Dremio, Athena, and Iceberg-based data lakes. This closes a long-standing gap, connecting SQL and Python, data engineering, science and analytics, and AI pipelines and the data they consume. AI agents for reliability, built into the workflow Elementary introduces agents that take on the operational reliability work while engineers keep ownership and approvals. Triage & Resolution: Investigates failures using lineage and incident history, identifies the cause, and drafts pull requests with proposed fixes. Coverage: Flags missing or insufficient tests, recommends the right ones, and prioritizes them based on downstream impact. Performance & Cost: Detects inefficient queries and pipelines and generates optimized SQL or configuration changes. CI Prevention (coming soon): Analyzes pull requests before merge, checks downstream impact, compares dev to prod assets, and prevents regressions from being deployed. Engineers decide the rules, guardrails, and approvals. The agents handle the heavy lifting. Code is (still) the way to scale From day one, we built a code-first experience. Reliability should be part of the development process, not an afterthought. You build data pipelines with engineering best practices like versioning, collaboration, and automation. Reliability should be treated the same way. Elementary’s source of truth is your codebase, which makes it scalable and maintainable. Our core is open-source packages that plug directly into your pipelines: dbt, and now Python as well. This lets data teams manage SQL, Python, and AI pipelines in a single platform, connecting data engineering and data science. In Elementary 2.0, this code-first experience gets a major upgrade: AI agents that code with you: Agents don’t just “assist”, they open pull requests and propose code changes alongside your team. An MCP server wired into your dev workflow: All Elementary context, tests, incidents, lineage, health, is available directly from your editor and tools that speak MCP. We meet engineers where they actually work: in code. Elementary 2.0 doubles down on that principle, while also introducing a new experience for business users. Bringing business users into the reliability loop Business users often feel data quality issues first, but until today, they have no real way to help improve them. As a result, data often lags behind the business, slowing down the very decisions it is meant to empower. Elementary is introducing an AI-first experience, allowing them to: Contribute data quality rules Discover and understand data Participate in governance Without needing engineering skills or new workflows. It connects their context to the same shared engine used by engineers and data scientists. Scaling data and AI products with confidence Elementary extends reliability across the entire data and AI lifecycle. By combining shared context with proactive AI agents, organizations can scale pipelines, data products, and AI initiatives without slowing down teams or increasing operational overhead. This is just the start. We will continue to expand integrations, deepen automation, and raise the baseline for how reliable data systems should work.
